meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you're not ready to die for it, take the word 'freedom' out of your vocabulary'?

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1925–1965 · Nation of Islam minister, then independent human rights leader
answer.sourceLine: The line is credited to Malcolm X everywhere, but Wikiquote lists it among his Attributed quotes — not in its sourced, year-organised sections — with a bare citation to the Chicago Defender of 28 November 1962 and no page, headline or facsimile. We could not produce that newspaper page, and the scholars who quote the sentence — Manning Marable and James H. Cone among them — print it with put the word ‘freedom’ out of your vocabulary, not take. What he demonstrably did say, closing “The Ballot or the Bullet” in Detroit on 12 April 1964, is the near-twin: “if you’re not ready to pay that price don’t use the word freedom in your vocabulary.”

source.excerpt: If you’re not ready to die for it, take the word “freedom” out of your vocabulary.
trail: Wikiquote carries this exact wording in its Attributed section — not in the year-by-year sourced sections, where the 1962 entries do not include it — cited to the Chicago Defender of 28 November 1962, a bare newspaper name and date with no headline or page. See the entry ↗.

Quote Investigator has never taken this one up. A search of the site returns no article, so there is no specialist tracing to defer to here — unusual for a line this widely circulated. Search result ↗.

One independent published source repeats the citation with its full date — Oliver McAdoo’s AS Critical Thinking for AQA gives “(Malcolm X, Chicago Defender, 28 November 1962)” — though as a 2000s textbook it may itself be drawing on Wikiquote. Full-text search ↗.

We checked the speech it is usually pinned to, and the answer is more interesting than a flat no. The word “vocabulary” is absent from the Cleveland text of 3 April 1964 ↗, but the Detroit delivery of 12 April 1964 closes with it: “It’ll be liberty or it’ll be death. And if you’re not ready to pay that price don’t use the word freedom in your vocabulary.” See the full Detroit transcript ↗. So the speech is not the source of the wording printed here — but it is the documented home of the same sentence in a different verb.
source.excerptNote: No fuller passage has been located. Wikiquote carries the sentence standing alone, and the surrounding text of whatever Chicago Defender item it came from — report, interview or speech coverage — has not been produced. The scholarly literature prints the same sentence alone too, with “put” in place of “take.”
source.rightsHolder: The Estate of Malcolm X; and, if the wording does originate in the Chicago Defender of 28 November 1962, that newspaper’s publisher
source.rightsNote: Nothing Malcolm X said or wrote can be public domain in the United States on age alone — he was born in 1925 and died in 1965, so every possible source postdates the pre-1931 first-publication cutoff. The best-cited home for this wording, a Chicago Defender item of 28 November 1962, sits firmly in copyright; and because that page has not been produced, we cannot even establish with certainty whose rights attach. Treat the line as in-copyright and quote it as a short quotation with attribution.

author.bio: Born Malcolm Little in Omaha, Nebraska, on 19 May 1925, he converted to the Nation of Islam in prison and rose to become its national spokesman, the movement’s sharpest and most quoted public voice. He broke with the Nation on 8 March 1964 and spent his last year building an independent Black internationalist politics, before he was assassinated in New York City on 21 February 1965. He was, by the early 1960s, one of the most heavily reported figures in American life — which is exactly why so many sentences he never quite said now travel under his name.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The problem here is not the man — it is the sentence, the source and a verb. Three separate things get mangled.

items.why: The version that circulates online reads “take the word ‘freedom’ out of your vocabulary.” The version in the serious literature — Manning Marable’s biography, James H. Cone’s Martin & Malcolm & America and Risks of Faith — reads “put the word ‘freedom’ out of your vocabulary.” The split is visible in full-text search ↗.

Quote pages routinely file this exact wording under Malcolm X’s most famous address, and that is wrong — but not by as much as it looks. The word “vocabulary” is nowhere in the Cleveland text of 3 April 1964 ↗. It is very much in the Detroit delivery of 12 April, which closes: “It’ll be liberty or it’ll be death. And if you’re not ready to pay that price don’t use the word freedom in your vocabulary.” Full Detroit transcript ↗. Cite that sentence and you are on firm ground; cite the “take the word ‘freedom’ out” version as a line from the speech and you are quoting something the transcripts do not contain.

The two get blended, and the blend is then presented as one quotation. But that second sentence is the well-documented one: Wikiquote traces it to a June 1964 television interview in New York City ↗. If you want a sourced Malcolm X line on this theme, use that one.

misattribution.truthLine: Nothing here suggests fabrication — the sentiment is Malcolm X’s to the bone, and he said a near-identical sentence on the record in Detroit on 12 April 1964. But Wikiquote itself files this wording under Attributed, not among its sourced quotations ↗, and the whole attribution hangs on one bare newspaper citation, the Chicago Defender of 28 November 1962, that nobody has yet put in front of a reader.

context.heading: Why a bare newspaper date is the whole story here
lead: This is not one of the easy cases where a famous name has been bolted onto a greeting-card sentiment. The thought is unmistakably Malcolm X’s — he said versions of it constantly, and one of them, “The price of freedom is death,” is documented to a June 1964 New York television interview ↗. What is shaky is the specific sentence the internet prints, and the single unexamined newspaper citation holding it up.

The sentence also has a documented near-twin, which most quote pages miss. Closing “The Ballot or the Bullet” in Detroit on 12 April 1964, Malcolm X said: “It’ll be liberty or it’ll be death. And if you’re not ready to pay that price don’t use the word freedom in your vocabulary.” It is there in the full Detroit transcript ↗, the same one Wikiquote cites. Same construction, same bargain, on the record — which makes the 1962 newspaper line look less like an invention than like a rougher cousin of a sentence he provably used.

Late 1962 is a plausible moment for it. Malcolm X had spent that year at his most confrontational, following the April 1962 Los Angeles police shooting that killed Nation of Islam member Ronald Stokes, and his remarks were being reported widely in print and on the air ↗. The Chicago Defender was then a daily paper — it had gone daily on 6 February 1956 as the Chicago Daily Defender ↗ — and it covered him closely. A quotation of his in its pages on 28 November 1962 is entirely believable. It has simply never been shown.
context.detailsSummary: The “take” / “put” split, and the book that does not contain it
detailsBody: Run the sentence through full-text search of scanned books and it splits cleanly in two. The form with take shows up in a prison-reform monograph and a British A-level critical-thinking textbook. The form with put shows up in the serious Malcolm X literature: Manning Marable’s Malcolm X: A Life of Reinvention, James H. Cone’s Martin & Malcolm & America and his Risks of Faith. You can see the split yourself ↗. When the scholars and the memes disagree about a verb, the memes are usually the ones that drifted.

One absence is worth noting. Malcolm X Speaks, George Breitman’s 1965 collection and the standard printed home of the major speeches, does not turn up in searches for either wording — although the same search engine surfaces it readily for other Malcolm X lines ↗, such as “You get freedom by letting your enemy know that you’ll do anything to get your freedom.” That is an observation about search results, not proof of absence — and it is unsurprising once you notice that the form Malcolm X is documented as speaking is neither of these two, but the “pay that price” sentence from Detroit.
